title: Design review deck — KV cache compaction + eviction (Serving Runtime)
content:
Redwood Inference — Serving Runtime
Design Review Deck
KV Cache Compaction Improvements (Allocator + Eviction + Scheduler Contract)

Presenter(s): Omar El-Sayed, Noah Patel
Reviewers requested: Sofia Ivanova (Scheduling), Hiro Tanaka (Kernels), Grace Kim (Kernel safety), Sean Gallagher (SRE), Allison Grant (Observability)
Date: 2025-03-04

---
Slide 1 — Title
KV Cache Compaction + Eviction: design review
Serving Runtime Performance — Kernel + Scheduling

Speaker notes:
- This is the v1 design review for online compaction + eviction policy changes.
- Goal is to reduce fragmentation-driven p95/p99 spikes and allocator churn under bursty mixed-length traffic.

---
Slide 2 — Agenda
1) Why we’re here (symptoms + incident tie-in)
2) Baseline: what fragmentation looks like in prod-like mixes
3) Proposed architecture: compaction-capable allocator + move semantics
4) Eviction policy and scheduler contract
5) Triggers + budgets (protect median latency)
6) Concurrency and safety model (kernel/stream constraints)
7) Observability + perf methodology
8) Rollout plan + rollback levers
9) Decisions needed + open questions

---
Slide 3 — Problem statement (what breaks today)
Symptoms we see in Hosted + some Dedicated pools:
- KV cache becomes fragmented under bursty arrivals + mixed context lengths
- allocator fast path slows (free list scan / block search)
- increases probability of expensive re-allocations and “allocation retries”
- p95/p99 spikes correlate with allocator churn and occasional OOM pressure
- conservative admission control kicks in earlier → throughput loss

Non-goals:
- Not rewriting entire attention cache subsystem
- Not changing model semantics
- Not building long-horizon defrag across device resets

Speaker notes:
- We are explicitly focusing on online compaction + eviction, not a full re-architecture.

---
Slide 4 — Incident context (Feb 11)
Postmortem: pm-2025-02-11-burst-tail-latency-kv-fragmentation
What happened:
- burst routing + mixed workloads
- fragmentation ratio climbed over ~45–55% in affected pools
- allocation failures increased → fallback behaviors + timeouts
- p99 worsened in short windows (spiky tails)
Immediate mitigations used:
- tightened admission control
- reduced max context for certain pools
- temporarily adjusted routing away from hot pools

Takeaway:
- mitigation is throughput-negative; we need runtime-level fix.

---
Slide 5 — Baseline: fragmentation under bursty mixes
From benchmark-lab + perf suite prototype runs (see ENG-2843):
- Worst-case mix: interleaved short chat + long-context summarization
- Fragmentation pattern: many small holes left by completed sequences; uneven block utilization
- Tail: spikes coincide with allocator “search time” and forced evictions

What we’re targeting:
- Reduce fragmentation ratio in steady state for mixed workloads
- Reduce allocation failure rate (per 1k req / per 1M tokens)
- Improve p95/p99 latency variance under bursts (esp decode)

Speaker notes:
- We’ll hold exact numbers out of the deck; focus on relative improvements + methodology.
- In canary we’ll use strict regression gates.

---
Slide 6 — Definitions (so we measure consistently)
KV cache uses block/page allocation.

Definitions (working):
- Total KV capacity (bytes): total bytes reserved for KV on GPU
- Used bytes: bytes holding active tokens for live sequences
- Free bytes: bytes available to allocate
- Fragmented bytes: bytes free but unusable for a request due to block shape/contiguity constraints
- Fragmentation ratio: fragmented_bytes / (free_bytes + fragmented_bytes)
- Allocation failure: allocator cannot satisfy request at current policy without eviction/compaction

Notes:
- “Fragmentation ratio” is not “utilization”; high utilization can be fine if free space is contiguous/usable.

---
Slide 7 — Design goals
Functional goals:
- Enable online compaction: reclaim holes by moving blocks/pages
- Integrate eviction that is scheduler-aware (fairness, backpressure)
- Preserve correctness under concurrent prefill/decode (multi-stream)

Performance goals:
- Protect median latency: compaction must be budgeted
- Tail reduction: reduce p95/p99 spikes attributable to allocator churn
- Avoid pathological thrash: prevent compaction/eviction oscillations under pressure

Ops goals:
- Feature-flagged rollout, safe defaults OFF
- Metrics that explain “why tail happened” (attribution)

---
Slide 8 — Proposed architecture (high level)
We introduce:
1) Compaction-capable block map allocator
2) Move engine (device-to-device copy + metadata updates)
3) Eviction policy v1 with scheduler contract
4) Trigger policy + budget enforcement
5) Telemetry: fragmentation + compaction cost + per-request annotations

Key constraint:
- Kernels must never dereference stale pointers; move must be synchronized with in-flight work.

---
Slide 9 — Allocator today vs proposed
Today:
- block/page allocator, free list tracking, limited ability to address holes
- eviction can free blocks but does not “pack” live blocks

Proposed:
- explicit block map with stable logical IDs
- physical placement may change (movable blocks)
- mapping (logical → physical) updated atomically at safe points

Diagram (conceptual):

Before (fragmented):
[ A A A ][ . . . ][ B B ][ . ][ C ][ . . ][ D D D ][ . ]

After (compacted):
[ A A A ][ B B ][ C ][ D D D ][ . . . . . . . . . . . ]

Legend: letters = live segments; '.' = free/holes

---
Slide 10 — Block size + move semantics (ADR-0127)
Decision points:
- Block/page size (e.g., 16–64 tokens worth of KV per head group)
- Whether blocks are movable (YES for v1)

Tradeoffs:
- Smaller blocks: less internal waste, more metadata + mapping overhead
- Larger blocks: less metadata, more internal fragmentation
- Movable blocks: enables compaction, but requires safe remap + kernel assumptions

Current proposal:
- Keep current page size (minimize kernel changes) + add movability behind flag
- Use indirection table for addressing (logical ID) where feasible

Speaker notes:
- This aligns with “prepare without behavior change” refactor (PR-18431).

---
Slide 11 — Data structures (block map abstraction)
Core structures:
- BlockMap: logical_block_id → physical_page_index
- PageState: {FREE, USED, MOVING}
- Allocation bitmap / free runs (fast search)
- SequenceKVIndex: per sequence, list of logical blocks holding its tokens

Key invariants:
- A logical block ID is stable for the lifetime of the token span it represents
- Physical pages can change, but only via move protocol
- Updates to mappings occur only at defined safe points (stream sync boundary)

---
Slide 12 — Move protocol (compaction engine)
Move = copy data + update mapping + release old page

Protocol sketch:
1) Select victim live page(s) to move (based on compaction plan)
2) Mark page MOVING (exclude from new allocations)
3) Ensure no in-flight kernel will read old physical address after update
   - synchronize on relevant CUDA stream(s) OR use per-page event fencing
4) Device-to-device copy old_page → new_page
5) Atomically update BlockMap mapping
6) Retire old page to FREE

Safety:
- No move if page is referenced by an in-flight decode step on an unsynchronized stream

Speaker notes:
- This is where Grace/Yuki feedback is needed: stream correctness and worst-case sync costs.

---
Slide 13 — When do we compact? (Trigger policy)
We do NOT run compaction continuously.
We compact when triggered and within budget.

Triggers (ADR-0128 proposal):
- Fragmentation ratio > threshold (per pool)
- Allocation pressure: allocation failure/retry rate above threshold
- “On allocation failure” fallback: try a small compaction burst before eviction escalation
- Optional: time-based (e.g., once per N seconds) only if already above minimum fragmentation

Anti-thrash guards:
- Cooldown window between compaction runs
- Stop compaction if median latency regression detected in window

---
Slide 14 — Budget model (protect median latency)
Budgets to enforce:
- Time budget per interval: e.g., X ms per second for compaction work
- Copy budget per interval: e.g., Y MB/s moved or Y pages per second
- Token budget proxy: cap compaction work relative to decode tokens served

Implementation detail:
- Compaction engine checks remaining budget before each move operation
- If budget exhausted → stop, leave system “partially compacted”

Why:
- Tail improvements are not worth regressing p50/p75 for everyone.

---
Slide 15 — Eviction policy v1 (what we evict, and why)
Eviction is distinct from compaction.
- Eviction: remove KV for a sequence (or prefix cache entry) so memory becomes free
- Compaction: rearrange live pages to reduce holes

Eviction policy goals:
- Avoid starving tenants / protect fairness
- Prefer evicting low-value KV (unlikely reuse, low SLA tier)
- Cooperate with scheduler: explicit signals and knobs

Victim selection factors (proposal):
- SLA / priority class (Hosted tier, Dedicated pool class)
- Request age / remaining tokens (avoid evicting near-complete if costly)
- Prefix-cache reuse probability (if integrated)
- Tenant fairness weight (avoid repeatedly evicting same tenant)

---
Slide 16 — Scheduler contract (ADR-0129)
We need a crisp contract between scheduler and KV cache.

Cache exports signals:
- cache_pressure_level: {0..3} derived from fragmentation + allocation failures
- eviction_cost_estimate: expected tokens to recompute if we evict (approx)
- compaction_active: boolean + current budget utilization

Scheduler provides inputs:
- request_priority_class: {interactive, batch, internal, canary} (example)
- tenant_fairness_weight / max_eviction_rate (optional)
- overload mode: {protect interactive, protect fairness, max throughput}

Scheduler behavior under pressure:
- may reduce concurrency / prefill admission
- may reorder work to reduce allocator churn

Speaker notes:
- Sofia/Lena/Julian: we need buy-in on the minimal contract v1 and how it affects scheduling heuristics.

---
Slide 17 — Allocator state diagram (simplified)
States:
- NORMAL: allocate from free runs, no compaction
- PRESSURE: elevated fragmentation or retries
- COMPACTING: compaction engine running within budget
- EMERGENCY: allocation failure persists; eviction escalates

State transitions:
NORMAL → PRESSURE when frag_ratio > T1 OR alloc_retry_rate > R1
PRESSURE → COMPACTING when budget available and cooldown passed
COMPACTING → NORMAL when frag_ratio < T0 OR budget exhausted and conditions cleared
COMPACTING → EMERGENCY when alloc failures persist and no progress
EMERGENCY → PRESSURE/NORMAL when pressure relieved

ASCII diagram:
NORMAL -> PRESSURE -> COMPACTING -> NORMAL
                 \-> EMERGENCY -> PRESSURE

---
Slide 18 — Compaction plan selection (how we pick moves)
Heuristic v1:
- Identify free runs at the “front” (low indices) and live pages behind holes
- Prefer moving smaller / colder pages first (reduce sync risk)
- Avoid moving pages tied to active decode steps if possible

Outcome:
- Fewer holes in hot allocation region
- Faster allocations (free runs become larger)

Note:
- We keep this heuristic intentionally simple for v1; tune based on canary.

---
Slide 19 — Concurrency model (what can run in parallel)
Concurrent components:
- Prefill kernels (new sequences allocate KV)
- Decode kernels (append tokens to existing KV)
- Eviction (may free KV pages)
- Compaction move engine (copies + remaps)

Safety constraints:
- No moving pages referenced by in-flight kernels on unsynchronized streams
- No remap while kernel can still read old address
- Allocation must see consistent BlockMap snapshot (RCU-like or lock + fast path)

Implementation approach (proposal):
- Fast path allocations use read-optimized structure
- Compaction uses coarse lock only around remap, not around scanning/planning

Speaker notes:
- We’ll validate via stress tests (ENG-2849) and include “rare race” reproducer coverage.

---
Slide 20 — Kernel implications (what changes / what must remain true)
Kernel-side assumptions to validate:
- Address calculation for KV reads/writes must tolerate indirection or stable physical pointers
- If we introduce indirection, cost must be negligible vs attention compute
- Stream sync boundaries: where is it safe to update mappings?

Mitigation strategy:
- Minimal kernel changes v1: keep existing addressing where possible
- Only enable movability where we can guarantee safe fences
- Provide kill switch: disable moves (compaction off) while keeping allocator refactor

---
Slide 21 — Expected impact (hypotheses)
We expect improvements in:
- Allocation search overhead under fragmentation
- Allocation failure rate under burst mixes
- p95/p99 stability (less spiky tails)
- OOM risk reduction (fewer emergency realloc patterns)

We expect some added overhead:
- Metadata updates + occasional stream fences
- Device-to-device copies during compaction

Guardrails:
- Budget enforcement prevents sustained overhead
- Canary gates protect p50/p75 regressions

---
Slide 22 — Metrics & logging (what we will ship)
New metrics (ENG-2842 / PR-18423 scope):
- kv_cache_fragmentation_ratio{region,pool,model_family}
- kv_cache_alloc_failures_total{region,pool,reason}
- kv_cache_alloc_retries_total
- kv_cache_compaction_moves_total
- kv_cache_compaction_bytes_moved_total
- kv_cache_compaction_time_ms_total (CPU) + (GPU) where available
- kv_cache_compaction_budget_exhausted_total
- kv_cache_evictions_total{policy,priority_class}

Structured logs (sample fields):
- request_id, tenant_id_hash, model, pool
- cache_pressure_level, eviction_action, compaction_action
- attribution: “tail candidate” marker when allocator stalls exceed threshold

---
Slide 23 — Dashboard mock (what oncall sees)
KV cache health dashboard panels (observability-pack PR-521):
- Fragmentation ratio over time (per region/pool)
- Allocation failures / retries (rate)
- Evictions per second, by priority class
- Compaction bytes moved + time (stacked)
- p95/p99 latency overlay (decode vs prefill)
- “Budget exhausted” events

What good looks like:
- frag ratio stays below T1 in steady state
- alloc failures near zero except during sharp burst
- compaction runs in short bursts; doesn’t correlate with p50 regression

---
Slide 24 — Perf methodology (how we prove it)
Perf suite additions (ENG-2843 / benchmark-lab PR-912):
- Bursty arrival process (Poisson bursts + quiet periods)
- Mixed sequence lengths (short chat, medium, long-context)
- Multi-tenant: skewed tenant distribution + fairness stress

Acceptance thresholds (draft):
- No >1–2% p50 regression in steady state
- p99 improvement target: meaningful reduction in tail spikes in burst scenario
- Allocation failure rate: reduced by X% vs baseline (finalize after baseline locked)

---
Slide 25 — Rollout plan (feature flag + canary)
Feature flags (ENG-2848 / PR-18469):
- enable_kv_compaction (default OFF)
- compaction_budget_ms_per_s
- compaction_bytes_per_s
- compaction_frag_threshold_T1 / T0
- eviction_mode (baseline vs v1)

Canary steps (ENG-2851):
1) Enable metrics/logging only everywhere (safe)
2) Enable allocator refactor (no behavior change)
3) Canary compaction in 1 hosted region + 1 dedicated pool
4) Expand to 25% traffic with strict gates (ENG-2852)
5) Broad rollout

Rollback:
- Disable compaction flag (immediate)
- Reduce budgets to near-zero (soft stop)
- Revert to baseline eviction mode

---
Slide 26 — Risk review (what could go wrong)
Top risks:
1) Kernel/stream safety bug → corruption / incorrect outputs
2) Compaction overhead regresses median latency under certain models
3) Thrash: repeated compaction + eviction oscillation under sustained pressure
4) Fairness regressions: same tenant gets repeatedly evicted
5) Observability blind spots: can’t attribute new tails

Mitigations:
- Stress tests with concurrency + random scheduling
- Kill switch + canary gating
- Conservative triggers + cooldowns
- Fairness constraints in victim selection + per-tenant caps
- Dashboards + alert thresholds agreed with SRE

---
Slide 27 — Open questions
Kernel addressing:
- Where do we enforce safe points for remap across all relevant streams?
- Do we need per-page event fencing vs global stream sync?

Eviction policy:
- How do we incorporate prefix-cache “reuse probability” without false positives?
- Which priority classes are truly protected (Hosted interactive vs batch)?

Scheduler contract:
- Minimal viable set of signals for v1 (avoid over-coupling)
- How should scheduler react at cache_pressure_level=3 (hard backpressure vs reroute)?

Threshold tuning:
- Default T1/T0 per pool type (Hosted vs Dedicated) and per model family

---
Slide 28 — Decisions requested from review
Decision A (ADR-0127):
- Confirm block size choice and allowing movable blocks behind flag

Decision B (ADR-0128):
- Approve trigger policy and budget model (time/bytes/cooldowns)

Decision C (ADR-0129):
- Approve scheduler/KV cache contract v1 (signals + required behaviors)

Decision D (Ops):
- Canary pools/regions selection and alert/rollback thresholds

---
Slide 29 — Appendix: detailed allocator states (for reviewers)
State: NORMAL
- allocations served from free runs
- eviction only on explicit policy / admission control

State: PRESSURE
- increase telemetry verbosity sampling
- begin planning compaction (no moves yet)
- request scheduler to reduce prefill admission (optional)

State: COMPACTING
- move operations executed within budget
- allocator continues serving requests; moves avoid active pages

State: EMERGENCY
- allow higher eviction aggressiveness
- scheduler enters overload mode; may reroute/reject

---
Slide 30 — Appendix: example “bad pattern” we want to eliminate
Observed pattern (conceptual):
- frag ratio climbs steadily during burst
- allocator retries spike
- evictions spike (but holes remain) → retry still high
- p99 spikes coincide with retry/eviction storm

Goal pattern:
- frag ratio triggers compaction early
- brief controlled bytes-moved burst
- frag ratio drops, retries remain low
- evictions only as needed, not stormy

---
Slide 31 — Appendix: sample alert thresholds (draft for SRE)
Draft alerts (to be tuned in canary):
- Warning: kv_cache_fragmentation_ratio > 0.45 for 10m (per pool)
- Page: kv_cache_alloc_failures_rate > baseline*2 for 5m AND p99 latency breach
- Page: compaction_budget_exhausted_rate high + persistent allocation failures (compaction not keeping up)
- Watch: compaction_time_ms_total correlates with p50 regression > 2% in window

Escalation:
- SRE oncall → runtime oncall if allocation failures persist > 15m

---
Slide 32 — Close
Success = fewer fragmentation-induced tail spikes without harming median.
Next steps:
- Capture review feedback on kernel safety + scheduler contract
- Finalize ADRs (0127–0129)
- Proceed to implementation phases + canary plan

Contact:
- Omar (allocator/compaction), Sofia (scheduler), Hiro/Grace (kernel safety), Sean (rollout)
